newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portugal parliament okays '97 budget outline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portugal parliament okays '97 budget outline.

text.p: Portugal's parliament on Friday approved the general terms of the 1997 budget after the main opposition Social Democrats (PSD) abstained so that the country would stay on track to join the European single currency.
The abstentions of the Social Democrats meant that the ruling Socialists' votes in favour were enough to guarantee a green light for the budget outline.
The budget forecasts a strong boost to revenues and a tight lid on spending to meet the tough entry test for joining the single currency in January 1999.

Parliament president Antonio Almeida Santos did not give the vote count, but said the Socialists voted in favour, the PSD abstained and the smaller rightwing anti-European Popular Party, Communist Party and Green Party voted against.
"We have decided not to block the budget," the PSD's parliamentary leader Luis Marques Mendes said earlier, winding up a three-day parliamentary debate.

"We have decided to let it go through not on the basis of its merit. It is an unjust budget because taxes will rise and it does not fight unemployment. We decided that the objective of the European single currency (which we support) was too serious to risk sparking a political crisis," he added.
Earlier this week, PSD leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa said in a press interview that the budget took the easy route to meeting single currency goals.
He accused the Socialists of ducking tough issues such as reform to the social security and health systems.

But he stopped short of saying his party, the largest in parliament after the Socialists, would vote against the budget package which is crucial to Portugal's hopes of winning a place in Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Prime Minister Antonio Guterres urged parliament to pass the budget, saying that not to do so would harm the confidence of financial markets and slow down public investment and the creation of jobs.
He said the PSD had no grounds for wanting to turn the budget debate into a vote of confidence in the government as the opposition party had said it did not want early elections.
"This budget should be approved by those who believe in Europe and in Portugal's place in the single currency, in the vanguard of European integration," he told parliament.
The prime minister has repeatedly pledged the government's determination to join the first wave of countries taking part in the single currency, or euro.
"This budget should be approved by those who believe in a solid budgetary policy, with the support of a strong economy and sustainable non-inflationary growth," Guterres said.

The 1997 budget proposals outlined savings of 200 billion escudos ($1.3 billion) compared with 1996, with the deficit narrowing to 2.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) from an expected four percent this year.
Portugal is trying to meet the European Union's requirement for it to cut the budget deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997 in order to qualify to join the single currency.
Parliament will discuss the finer details of the budget before holding a final vote on December 11.
The budget is set to be passed in the final vote after the PSD's pledge on Friday not to derail it.
The Socialists have 112 seats in the 230-seat parliament against 88 for the PSD. The remainder are split between the anti-European PP, the Communists and the Green Party.
